about: Sift's knowledge base: the single source for the Help page, the hover explanations and the Word glossary. Edit here, then rebuild the Word document (scripts/build_rules_doc.js). {placeholders} take the live thresholds.

entries.title: Getting around Sift
entries.definition: What each page in the menu bar is for.
body: Dashboard: the home page. What needs your attention, what changed overnight, the top opportunities and how the track record is going.

Screener: every company Sift values, with its score, margin of safety, the four value tests and a suggested action. Filter by action, sector, watchlist or held shares; click a heading to sort and a row to open the company.

ETFs: every ETF on the ASX, kept apart from shares, with its fee, size, yield and returns. Click one for its page: performance against its category and a fund you choose, growth of $10,000, distributions and fund facts.
LICs: every listed investment company and trust on the ASX, kept apart from shares and ETFs, with the share price against net tangible assets (NTA), fee, yield and returns.
Company pages: the score wheel and its 30 checks, price against estimated value, the four value tests, quality markers, red flags, key ratios and charts of price, margin of safety and the financials.
Watchlists and Portfolios: your lists of companies to follow, and your holdings with trades and CGT records.
Track record: whether Sift's suggestions have actually worked.

Coattail: follow the smart money. The fund managers holding the screener's companies, as cards you can open, and which companies they're adding to and cutting, with ASX director trades and substantial holders to come.
Help: this page. Hover any underlined heading or label in Sift for a short explanation; on a phone, tap the small i.
Model and rules (avatar menu, admins): every setting and formula, what-if scenarios and Users.
Search: the box at the top right finds anything in Sift, everywhere or just on the page you're on (the pink ▾ chooses). Results can be narrowed with tick boxes down the left.

entries.title: Data date and the nightly refresh
entries.definition: The chip next to the search box shows the date of the latest prices and valuations, refreshed by a job each night.
body: Each night at 6 pm the scheduled job updates the database schema, downloads prices and financial statements, collects ETF prices and distributions (and, once a month, the ASX's ETF report), recalculates every valuation, records that night's signals, scores earlier signals whose results are due, and writes the action report.

The chip is green when the data is current. It turns amber with a ! when the latest valuations are older than the last weekday's close (the job didn't run, or it was a public holiday) or when the last run crashed or didn't finish. Hover it to see when the last run started and finished and how many companies it couldn't update; a few each night is normal.

A run that didn't finish, with a log that just stops and no error, was almost always ended from outside Sift: Task Scheduler stopping it when the PC stopped being idle, its window being closed, or the PC sleeping. The README's Daily Automation section has the settings that prevent this; each step in the log shows when it started and how long it took.
If a page shows Could not load, the message under it says why. A message about a missing table or column means the database needs updating: restart python gui.py, or run python -m src.apply_schema.

entries.title: Dashboard
entries.definition: The home page: what needs attention, what changed and where the opportunities are.
entries.hover: Units held x latest closing price, across every open parcel recorded with portfolio.py.
body: Portfolio strip: value at the latest close, today's change, unrealised gain and cost base across every portfolio.
Needs attention: held shares flagged SELL or REVIEW, parcels reaching the CGT discount within 90 days, held shares missing from the nightly ticker file, and watchlist triggers met.

What changed: companies whose suggested action moved since the previous night. Watchlist companies come first, then better moves. A move between actions of equal rank, or one caused by your own buying or selling, isn't listed.

Biggest movers: the 5 screener shares that rose most and the 5 that fell most on the last trading day, by percentage change from the previous close, each with its score wheel, then the top 5 each way for ETFs and for LICs. Only prices from that day count, so a suspended stock's old move isn't shown. No price or volume floor: a very cheap stock can top the list.
Top opportunities: up to six shares you don't hold, BUY first then INVESTIGATE, by score and margin of safety.
Today's suggested actions: counts per action; click one to open the screener filtered to it.

Arranging the widgets: each widget has a pin at its top right and starts pinned. Click the pin to unlock it, then drag it by its title bar (mouse or finger), or use the arrows, switch it between half and full width, or hide it. Click the pin again to lock it. Hidden widgets are listed under the dashboard with a Show button, and Reset to default layout puts everything back. The layout is saved in Sift's database, so every browser and your phone show the same; widgets are pinned again each time the page opens.
ETFs: watchlist triggers met on ETFs, ETF parcels reaching the CGT discount, and the ETFs you hold or watch with today's move, 1-year return and yield.
LICs: the same for listed investment companies and trusts, with each one's premium or discount to NTA.

entries.title: Margin of safety
entries.definition: How far the share price sits below intrinsic value. A buffer against errors in the estimate.
entries.hover: How far the price sits below estimated intrinsic value: (value - price) / value. Positive means cheaper than estimated value; negative means dearer. Passes the value test above {margin_of_safety}%.

entries.title: Estimated value
entries.definition: Sift's estimate of intrinsic value per share, from a discounted cash flow model, or a dividend discount model for banks, insurers and REITs.
entries.hover: Intrinsic value per share from the company's valuation model. Hover the bar label in the chart below for the model's full assumptions.

entries.title: Intrinsic value
entries.definition: The estimated value of a share based on the cash it is expected to generate, independent of the market price.

entries.title: Valuation status
entries.definition: Where the price sits against estimated value: Undervalued, Fair value, Overvalued or No estimate.
entries.hover: Where the price sits against estimated value. Undervalued: margin of safety above {margin_of_safety}% (passes the value test). Fair value: 0% to {margin_of_safety}%. Overvalued: below 0%, so the price is above estimated value. No estimate: no valuation model could run.

entries.title: Implied upside
entries.definition: How much the share price would need to rise to reach estimated value: (estimated value - price) / price.
entries.hover: How much the price would rise to reach estimated value: (value - price) / price. Not the same as margin of safety, which divides by value: a 40% margin of safety is a 67% implied upside.

entries.title: Graham Number
entries.definition: Benjamin Graham's ceiling price: the square root of 22.5 x earnings per share x book value per share.
entries.hover: Benjamin Graham's ceiling on what a defensive investor should pay: the square root of 22.5 x earnings per share x book value per share. 22.5 is his maximum P/E of 15 times his maximum P/B of 1.5, so a price below it means both limits are met at once. Uses the latest annual report; blank if earnings or book value is negative. One of the score wheel's Value checks, but not used in the four value tests or the action. It ignores growth, so it understates companies with few physical assets.

entries.title: Discounted cash flow (DCF)
entries.definition: Valuation that converts expected future free cash flows into today's dollars.
entries.hover: Intrinsic value per share from a two-stage discounted cash flow (DCF) model: average free cash flow over the last three years, grown at 8% a year for five years and 2.5% a year after that, discounted back at 9% a year. Cash is added and debt subtracted, then the total is divided by shares on issue. This is the figure the margin of safety and the value test use.

entries.title: Dividend discount model (DDM)
entries.definition: Valuation that converts expected future dividends into today's dollars. Used for financials and property.
entries.hover: Intrinsic value per share from a two-stage dividend discount model (DDM), used for banks, insurers and REITs because their free cash flow isn't meaningful: average dividend per share over the last three years, grown at 5% a year for five years and 2.5% a year after that, discounted back at 9% a year. This is the figure the margin of safety and the value test use.

entries.title: Discount rate
entries.definition: The annual return required to justify the investment, used to convert future cash into today's dollars. 9% in this tool.

entries.title: Terminal value
entries.definition: The value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period, assuming steady growth thereafter.

entries.title: Share price
entries.definition: The latest closing price on the ASX.
entries.hover: Latest closing price on the ASX. The further it sits below the estimated value, the larger the margin of safety.

entries.title: Price
entries.definition: The latest closing share price on the ASX.
entries.hover: Latest closing share price on the ASX.

entries.title: Return on equity (ROE)
entries.definition: Net profit as a percentage of shareholders' equity.
entries.hover: Return on equity: net profit after tax / shareholders' equity. How well the company earns on its owners' money. Passes the value test above {roe}%.

entries.title: Return on invested capital (ROIC)
entries.definition: Net profit as a percentage of debt plus equity, less cash.
entries.hover: Return on invested capital: net profit / (debt + equity - cash). The return on all the capital the business uses, not just shareholders' money.

entries.title: Debt to equity
entries.definition: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity. Lower means less financial risk.
entries.hover: Total debt / shareholders' equity. Lower means less financial risk. Passes the value test below {debt_to_equity}.

entries.title: Price-to-earnings ratio (P/E)
entries.definition: Share price divided by EPS.
entries.hover: Price-to-earnings ratio: share price / earnings per share. Lower can mean cheaper. Graham's ceiling was 15.

entries.title: Price-to-book ratio (P/B)
entries.definition: Share price divided by book value per share.
entries.hover: Price-to-book ratio: share price / book value (equity) per share. Graham's ceiling was 1.5.

entries.title: Price to free cash flow
entries.definition: Share price divided by free cash flow per share.
entries.hover: Share price / free cash flow per share, latest year. Lower means more cash generated for each dollar paid.

entries.title: EV/EBIT
entries.definition: Enterprise value divided by earnings before interest and tax.
entries.hover: Enterprise value (market capitalisation + debt - cash) / earnings before interest and tax. Compares companies regardless of how they are funded.

entries.title: Enterprise value (EV)
entries.definition: Market capitalisation plus debt minus cash: the value of the whole business.

entries.title: Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT)
entries.definition: Operating profit before financing costs and tax.

entries.title: Earnings per share (EPS)
entries.definition: Net profit after tax divided by shares on issue.

entries.title: Free cash flow (FCF)
entries.definition: Operating cash flow less capital expenditure: the cash available to shareholders.

entries.title: Book value
entries.definition: Total shareholders' equity from the balance sheet. Per share: equity divided by shares on issue.

entries.title: Shares on issue
entries.definition: The total number of a company's shares held by investors.

entries.title: Percentage point
entries.definition: The simple difference between two percentages. Moving from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 percentage points.

entries.title: Grossed-up dividend yield
entries.definition: Dividend yield including the value of franking credits.
entries.hover: Dividend yield including franking credits: cash dividend x (1 + franking % x 30/70) / price. Companies based outside Australia are treated as unfranked. Passes the value test above {yield}%. Ordinary dividends only: a one-off payment more than twice the usual annual dividend is excluded.

entries.title: Cash dividend yield
entries.definition: Cash dividend divided by share price, before franking credits.
entries.hover: Cash dividend / share price, before franking credits. Ordinary dividends only: a one-off payment more than twice the usual annual dividend is excluded.

entries.title: Franking credit
entries.definition: A credit for company tax already paid on a dividend, which Australian resident shareholders can offset against their own tax.

entries.title: Payout ratio
entries.definition: The share of earnings paid out as dividends.
entries.hover: Dividend / earnings per share. Above 100% the dividend exceeds profit; above 150% it is flagged as a likely one-off. Ordinary dividends only: a one-off payment more than twice the usual annual dividend is excluded.

entries.title: Abnormal distribution
entries.definition: A one-off payment more than twice the usual annual dividend, such as a capital return or a very large special dividend. Excluded from all dividend figures (see section 3).

entries.title: Capital return
entries.definition: Money paid back to shareholders out of the company's capital rather than its profits, sometimes by cancelling a portion of shares. Not a dividend, though data feeds sometimes record it as one.

entries.title: Ex-dividend date
entries.definition: The date from which a buyer of the share no longer receives the next dividend. Used to assign each payment to a financial year.

entries.title: Dividend trend
entries.definition: Whether ordinary dividends are GROWING, STEADY, CUT or NONE over up to five years.
entries.hover: Over up to five years. CUT: the latest dividend is more than 10% below last year's or the earlier median. GROWING: more than 5% above the oldest. STEADY otherwise. NONE: pays no dividend. Ordinary dividends only: a one-off payment more than twice the usual annual dividend is excluded.

entries.title: Dividend reinvestment plan (DRP)
entries.definition: Dividends paid as new shares instead of cash. Each reinvestment creates a new parcel.

entries.title: Four value tests
entries.definition: The core screen: margin of safety above {margin_of_safety}%, ROE above {roe}%, debt to equity below {debt_to_equity} and grossed-up yield above {yield}%.
entries.hover: The four core value tests, in order: margin of safety, ROE, debt/equity, grossed-up yield. A tick passes; a cross fails or has no data. All four must pass for an overall pass.
body: All four must pass for an overall pass. A missing figure never counts as a pass.
The suggested action builds on these tests, then checks red flags and trends.

entries.title: Suggested action
entries.definition: A research prompt from the rules for each company; not financial advice.
entries.hover: Suggested next step from the rules; the reason is on the company page. Shares you don't hold: BUY, INVESTIGATE, WATCH, AVOID, IGNORE. Shares you hold: SELL, REVIEW, ACCUMULATE, HOLD. A research prompt, not financial advice.
body: Shares you don't hold:
BUY: passes all four value tests with no red flags.
INVESTIGATE: passes all four but has a red flag to check, or is cheap and passes three of the four.
WATCH: cheap but fails two or more tests, getting cheaper quickly, or passes the other three tests while the price isn't cheap yet.
AVOID: looks cheap, but fundamentals are declining and profit isn't backed by cash.
IGNORE: no value signal.
Shares you hold:
SELL: fundamentals declining, plus trading above estimated value, weak earnings quality or a dividend cut.
REVIEW: a red flag, or the price is now well above estimated value.
ACCUMULATE: still meets the BUY standard (all four tests, no red flags), so adding is reasonable.
HOLD: no red flags, but doesn't pass all four tests, so not adding.

A SELL or REVIEW also notes when waiting a few weeks would bring parcels into the CGT discount. Every action's reason is on the company page, and the track record checks how each action has actually done.

entries.title: Accumulate
entries.definition: Add to a share you already hold. Suggested only when the share still meets the same standard as a new BUY.

entries.title: Red flag
entries.definition: A condition that downgrades an otherwise attractive result (see section 9).
body: The red flags: value-trap risk, a payout ratio over 150% (a likely one-off dividend), weak earnings quality, a dividend cut not yet restored, a price still making new lows, and low data confidence.

entries.title: Score wheel
entries.definition: A five-spoke chart in the web interface; each spoke counts how many of six yes/no checks a company passes (see section 11.2).
entries.hover: Score wheel total out of 30. Five spokes (Value, Performance, Health, Dividend, Momentum), each counting six yes/no checks. Higher is better. Open a company to see every check.
body: Value: margin of safety above 0%, above 20% and above 40%; P/E between 0 and 15; P/B between 0 and 1.5; price below the Graham Number.
Performance: ROE above 12% and above 20%; ROIC above 10%; fundamentals not DECLINING; earnings quality STRONG or ADEQUATE, and STRONG.
Health: debt to equity below 0.8 and below 0.4; cash at least equal to debt; positive equity, free cash flow and net profit.
Dividend: pays a dividend; grossed-up yield above 4.5% and above 6%; payout ratio 100% or less; dividend trend STEADY or GROWING, and GROWING.
Momentum: price trend UPTREND; not at new lows; in the upper half of the 52-week range; margin of safety trend above zero; momentum above 5 points; fundamentals IMPROVING.
The wheel describes a company; it doesn't decide the suggested action.

entries.title: Company
entries.definition: ASX code and company name. HELD marks shares you own; a pink star marks companies on your watchlists.
entries.hover: ASX code and company name. HELD marks shares you own.

entries.title: Sector
entries.definition: Industry sector from Yahoo Finance, which also decides the valuation model.
entries.hover: Industry sector from Yahoo Finance. Financial Services and Real Estate are valued with a dividend discount model; every other sector with a discounted cash flow model.

entries.title: Earnings quality
entries.definition: Operating cash flow as a share of net profit: STRONG, ADEQUATE or WEAK.
entries.hover: Operating cash flow / net profit over the last three years. STRONG at 100% or more, ADEQUATE 80% to 99%, WEAK below 80%. Profit that isn't turning into cash is a warning sign. Not assessed for banks, insurers and REITs.

entries.title: Price signal
entries.definition: The price trend: UPTREND, DOWNTREND or NEW LOWS, from the 200-day average and the 52-week range.
entries.hover: Price trend. UPTREND: at or above the 200-day average. DOWNTREND: below it. NEW LOWS: below it and in the bottom 10% of the 52-week range. Needs 200 days of prices.

entries.title: Fundamentals trend
entries.definition: Whether ROE and revenue are IMPROVING, STABLE or DECLINING across the last three annual reports.
entries.hover: Latest versus oldest of the last three annual reports. DECLINING: ROE down more than 2 points or revenue down more than 5%. IMPROVING: up by those amounts. STABLE otherwise. Ignores the share price.

entries.title: Margin of safety trend
entries.definition: Change in margin of safety over 30 days, in percentage points.
entries.hover: Change in margin of safety over the last 30 days, in percentage points. Positive means the share is getting cheaper relative to its estimated value. More than 5 points counts as momentum.

entries.title: Momentum (into value)
entries.definition: A widening margin of safety: the share is getting cheaper relative to its estimated value.

entries.title: Value trap
entries.definition: A share that looks cheap because its business is deteriorating, not because the market has mispriced it.
entries.hover: Yes when the margin of safety passes but fundamentals are DECLINING: the share looks cheap, possibly for a good reason.

entries.title: Data confidence
entries.definition: How complete a company's inputs are: HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
entries.hover: How complete the inputs are, from 11 checks (price, market capitalisation, profit, revenue, equity, debt, cash flows, years of reports, days of prices). HIGH: 10 or 11. MEDIUM: 8 or 9. LOW: 7 or fewer.

entries.title: 200-day moving average
entries.definition: The average of the last 200 daily closing prices. A common gauge of the longer-term price trend.

entries.title: 52-week range
entries.definition: The lowest to highest closing price over the past year.

entries.title: Portfolios and tax types
entries.definition: Several portfolios, each with its owner's tax type, which sets its CGT discount.
body: Individual and trust: 50% CGT discount. Self-managed super fund: 33 1/3%. Company: none.
Create a portfolio from Portfolios, + New portfolio. Each has its own holdings, sales and CGT report.
Archive a portfolio once everything in it is sold: its sales stay in the CGT report. A portfolio with sales can't be deleted, because sale records are kept for five years.
A company counts as held, for the suggested actions, if any portfolio holds it.
Each portfolio shows its shares, ETFs and LICs under separate headings, each with its own subtotal, above the combined total. ETF and LIC parcels are bought, sold and taxed the same way as shares.

entries.title: Recording trades
entries.definition: Record buys and sales on a portfolio's page, or with portfolio.py.
body: Buy: company, units, price, date and brokerage (added to the cost base), plus how it was acquired.
Sell: choose oldest parcels first, smallest taxable gain first (counting the portfolio's CGT discount), or one parcel. Part of a parcel can be sold; the rest stays open with its cost base intact.
Mistakes: Delete removes an open parcel entered in error; Undo reverses a sale. Both ask first.
Records are a tax aid, not tax advice.

entries.title: Parcel
entries.definition: A single acquisition of shares, tracked separately for tax.

entries.title: Cost base
entries.definition: The purchase value of a parcel plus buying brokerage.
entries.hover: What the shares still held cost: purchase price plus brokerage, the starting point for capital gains tax (CGT).

entries.title: Capital proceeds
entries.definition: The sale value of a parcel less selling brokerage.

entries.title: Capital gains tax (CGT)
entries.definition: Tax on the gain made when an asset, such as a share parcel, is sold.

entries.title: CGT discount
entries.definition: The 50% reduction in a capital gain for individuals and trusts on shares held for more than 12 months.
entries.hover: The first date a sale qualifies for the capital gains tax (CGT) discount: the day after the parcel has been held for 12 months.

entries.title: First in, first out (FIFO)
entries.definition: Sell order that disposes of the oldest parcel first.

entries.title: Financial year (FY)
entries.definition: A company's annual reporting period. For tax purposes, 1 July to 30 June.

entries.title: Australian Taxation Office (ATO)
entries.definition: Sets the capital gains tax rules applied to your holdings.

entries.title: Self-managed super fund (SMSF)
entries.definition: A superannuation fund run by its own members. Gets a 33⅓% CGT discount on assets held over 12 months.

entries.title: Watchlists and triggers
entries.definition: Named lists of companies and ETFs to follow without owning them, each with an optional note and triggers.
body: Add a company, ETF or LIC with the star at the left of its row in the screener, ETF or LIC list (☆ adds, ★ means it's on a list; either opens the list picker), with Add to watchlist on its page, or from the watchlist's own page.

Triggers: price at or below $Y for any; margin of safety above X% for shares; yield above X% for ETFs and LICs (the 12-month yield); discount to NTA of at least X% for LICs. A trigger met shows a tick on the watchlist page and appears on the dashboard while it stays true: share triggers under Needs attention, ETF and LIC triggers in their own cards.
Each watchlist shows its shares, ETFs and LICs under separate headings, with the figures that suit each.
Watched companies, ETFs and LICs show a pink ★ at the left of their row in the screener and the ETF and LIC lists (hover for the list names); each list can filter to one watchlist or to any.
Only companies Sift values, and ETFs it follows, can be watched. Watchlists are separate from the nightly ticker file (allords.txt), which decides which companies are valued.

entries.title: Track record
entries.definition: Whether Sift's suggestions have worked: each month's calls scored after 1, 3, 6 and 12 months.
body: Each company's first signal of each month is scored on its total return, dividends included, against the average of every company screened that night.
Confidence: too early under 30 signals, moderate from 30 to 100, solid above 100. The order check asks whether BUY beat WATCH and WATCH beat AVOID.

What did I miss lists BUY and INVESTIGATE calls you didn't buy within 30 days that beat the average by more than 10 points. What should I look at now lists today's signals of a kind that has proven itself, still more than 20% below estimated value.
Daily detail is kept for 14 months; monthly results are kept for good. Filter by rules version to judge each set of rules on its own results.

entries.title: Signal
entries.definition: What Sift said about a company on a given night: its suggested action, valuation status, estimated value and score, recorded for the track record (see section 11.4).

entries.title: Excess return
entries.definition: Total return including dividends, minus the average for every company screened the same night, in percentage points.

entries.title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
entries.definition: Australia's main stock exchange. The companies screened are listed here.

entries.title: New York Stock Exchange (NYSE)
entries.definition: The largest stock exchange in the United States.

entries.title: Exchange traded fund (ETF)
entries.definition: A fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share, usually tracking an index.
body: Sift collects every ETF listed on the ASX: its fund facts each month from the ASX Investment Products report, and its prices and distributions each night.

ETFs aren't valued like companies. A fund has no cash flow or dividend policy of its own to value, so ETFs are left out of the estimated value, the four value tests, the score wheel and the track record, and are judged on cost, size, distributions and performance instead.

Performance is Sift's own total return: one unit bought at the start, each distribution reinvested at the close on its ex-date, valued at the latest close. Periods over a year are shown as a yearly rate. It's measured from the prices actually traded, so distributions are counted once.

Each month Sift also measures the 1-year return at the report's month end and sets it beside the ASX's own figure. A gap of more than 2 points usually means a missing distribution or a bad price, or a report figure worked out a different way.
entries.hover: An exchange traded fund: one trade buys a slice of many investments. Judged on fee, size, distributions and total return, not estimated value.

entries.title: ASX Investment Products report
entries.definition: The ASX's monthly list of every exchange traded product, with its issuer, category, fees, size, flows, spread and performance. Sift's source for which ETFs exist and their fund facts.
body: The ASX publishes it each month, usually by the seventh business day of the next month. Each night until last month's report is loaded, Sift looks for it: first in the data/asx_reports folder, then on the ASX website. Once it's loaded, nothing is downloaded until the next month.

Its returns (1 month, 1, 3 and 5 years) come from Bloomberg with dividends reinvested gross, that is including franking credits. Sift's own returns count cash distributions only, so for a franked Australian fund the ASX figure is usually a little higher. Each ETF's page shows both.

Every ETF it lists is added to Sift with its category (the report's section headings, such as Equity - Australia), issuer, fee, size, flows, spread and yield; one it no longer lists is marked inactive and its history is kept. Listed investment companies and trusts (LICs and LITs), A-REITs, infrastructure funds and the benchmark index rows are left out. Funds marked ^ invest in other ETFs, which the ETF's page notes.

If the download doesn't work, save the spreadsheet from the ASX website into data/asx_reports and the next nightly run loads it. To check how a file is read without loading it, run python -m src.etf.run_etfs --inspect followed by the file name.
entries.hover: The returns in the ASX's monthly report, to its month end, from Bloomberg. They include franking credits (gross dividends reinvested), so for franked Australian funds they run a little above Sift's cash-only figures.

entries.title: Checking returns against the ASX report
entries.definition: Each night Sift measures every ETF's and LIC's returns again to the month end of the latest ASX report and compares them with the report's own figures. A period that doesn't agree is marked ⚠ rather than shown as a confident bar.
body: A period is marked when Sift's return to the report's month end differs from the ASX's by more than 2 points. The ASX counts franking credits, so an Australian equity fund's ASX figure runs higher; for those a shortfall of up to 4 points is expected and not marked.

A period is also marked when the price history inside it has a one-day move of more than 40%. Funds don't move that much in a day: it's an unadjusted split or consolidation, a currency change in the price feed, or a bad price, and every return measured across it is wrong.

A marked figure stays in the table with ⚠ and the reason, but is left off the chart and out of the category average. Since first price is checked only when Sift's prices start near the fund's listing date, since the ASX measures it from listing.

On the Performance chart only yearly rates (1, 3, 5 and 10 years) are drawn, so every bar is the same unit. Recent returns (1, 3 and 6 months) are not annualised and are listed under the chart; since first price is in the table with each fund's own start date and isn't averaged, because funds in a category start on different dates.

The check shows as one line above the Performance chart: a tick when every period agrees, or the list of figures to check. The ASX's own figures aren't shown as a column, because they're the same fund to a different date, not a comparison.

entries.title: Against its index
entries.definition: For Australian share and property funds, the fund's return beside its market index (such as the S&P/ASX 200 Accumulation), both from the ASX report to its month end.
body: Both figures come from the same report and the same date and both count franking credits, so the difference is a fair comparison: for an index fund it should be a little below zero, about the fee; for an active fund or LIC it's what the manager added or lost.

The ASX report carries index returns for Australian indices only (the S&P/ASX 200, Small Ordinaries, A-REIT and Infrastructure accumulation indices), so global funds have no index comparison; compare them with a fund such as VGS or IVV instead.

entries.title: What a fund holds
entries.definition: An ETF's description, asset mix (shares, bonds, cash), top 10 holdings and sector weightings, and for bond funds their credit ratings and duration, from Yahoo Finance's fund data (supplied by Morningstar).
body: Sift fetches it weekly, a seventh of the funds each night; Yahoo updates holdings monthly or quarterly, so they can be a few weeks old. Coverage of ASX funds varies: some show everything, some only a description.
The top 10's share of the fund shows how concentrated it is: a broad index fund's top 10 might be 25%, a concentrated or thematic fund's 60% or more.
Duration is how sensitive a bond fund is to interest rates: with a duration of 5 years, a 1 point rise in rates lowers its value by about 5%.

LICs: Yahoo lists them as companies, so Sift shows their description but no holdings or sectors. Each LIC names its top holdings in its monthly NTA report, on its website or the ASX announcements page.

entries.title: ETF screener
entries.definition: Every ETF Sift follows, with its fee, size, returns and yield, kept apart from the share screener.
body: Click a heading to sort and a row to open the ETF. Search covers codes, names and the index a fund tracks.
Filter by category (the ASX's grouping, such as Australian Equities or Fixed Income), by issuer, by watchlist, or to the ETFs you hold.
Returns are Sift's own total returns with distributions reinvested; 3, 5 and 10 years are yearly rates. A blank means the fund is younger than the period.
There are no suggested actions or scores for ETFs: those come from estimated value, which a fund doesn't have.

entries.title: An ETF's page
entries.definition: Everything about one ETF: its price, fee, size and yield, performance against its category and a fund you choose, growth of $10,000, distributions and fund facts.
body: Performance: each period's total return beside the category average and a reference fund. The reference starts as the largest other fund in the same category; pick any ETF to compare instead.
Growth of $10,000: what $10,000 invested at the start of the period would be worth now, distributions reinvested, for this ETF and the reference fund over the same dates.
Unit price: the last 12 months, with D on each distribution's ex-date. Distributions per unit: each financial year's cash per unit.
Fund facts come from the latest ASX report; fund size over time appears once two months of reports are loaded.
If Sift's 1-year return differs from the ASX report's by more than 2 points, the page says so: usually a distribution Yahoo missed, or the ASX working it out another way.

entries.title: Fee (MER)
entries.definition: The fund's yearly cost as a percent of what you have invested, taken out of the fund's assets, so it's already reflected in the unit price and returns.
entries.hover: Yearly management fee as a percent of your investment (the MER). 0.10% costs $10 a year on $10,000. Already taken out of the returns shown.

entries.title: Fund size (FUM)
entries.definition: The total value of the fund's investments, from the ASX report. Larger funds tend to trade more easily and are less likely to close.
entries.hover: Total funds under management, from the latest ASX report. Larger funds usually trade with tighter spreads and are less likely to be closed.

entries.title: Bid/ask spread
entries.definition: The average gap between the best buying and selling prices on the ASX, as a percent of the price: a cost paid on every trade.
entries.hover: Average gap between the best bid and ask, as a percent of price (from the ASX report). A cost you pay each time you buy or sell.

entries.title: Net flows
entries.definition: Money invested into the fund less money taken out, over the report month. Rising flows mean investors are adding to it.

entries.title: Total return
entries.definition: The gain over a period counting both the price change and every distribution, reinvested on its ex-date. Over a year, shown as a yearly rate.
entries.hover: Price change plus distributions, reinvested at the ex-date close. 1 to 10 years are yearly rates; 1, 3 and 6 months are not annualised. Blank: the fund is younger than the period. Worked out by Sift from daily prices.

entries.title: Yield (12 months)
entries.definition: Cash distributions per unit with ex-dates in the last 12 months, as a percent of the latest unit price. Franking credits aren't included.
entries.hover: Distributions paid in the last 12 months divided by the latest price. All distributions count, including year-end distributions of gains. Before franking.

entries.title: Unit price
entries.definition: The latest closing price of one unit of the ETF on the ASX.

entries.title: Day move
entries.definition: The change in the unit price from the previous close to the latest close, in percent.

entries.title: Category
entries.definition: What the fund invests in, as the ASX groups it (for example Australian Equities, Global Equities, Fixed Income). Category averages compare funds within one category.

entries.title: Issuer
entries.definition: The company that manages the ETF, such as Vanguard, BlackRock (iShares) or Betashares.

entries.title: Category median and rank
entries.definition: Where a fund's return sits among the other funds in its ASX category, for each period: its rank (1st is best) out of the funds with a figure, and the category's middle (median) return.
body: Rank reads at a glance: 2nd of 33, top 10% means only one fund in the category did better. The bands (top 10%, top quarter, top half, bottom half, bottom quarter) come from the share of the other funds that did better, and aren't shown for categories of fewer than five funds.
The median is the middle fund's return, drawn on the chart. Unlike an average, one extreme fund (a leveraged or crypto fund in a wild year) can't drag it.

Keep in mind how broad a category is: Equity - Global holds US tech, whole-world, emerging market, small company, currency-hedged and themed funds. A high rank there says the fund did well among very different funds, not that it beat a like-for-like alternative. For that, compare with a specific fund.
Figures that fail their checks against the ASX report are left out of both. Since first price isn't ranked, because funds start on different dates.

entries.title: Reference fund
entries.definition: Another fund to compare against on an ETF's or LIC's page. It starts as the broad, low-cost alternative for the category (VAS for Australian shares, VGS for global shares, VAF for Australian bonds and so on), or the category's largest fund where there's no obvious one; choose any fund instead.

entries.title: Listed investment company (LIC)
entries.definition: An ASX-listed company whose business is investing in other shares.
entries.hover: A listed investment company or trust: a fund that trades on the ASX like a share, with a fixed number of shares, so its price can sit above or below the value of what it holds (its NTA).
body: Sift follows every LIC and LIT in the ASX's monthly Investment Products report, under its own LICs heading, apart from shares and ETFs. An LIC in the nightly ticker file is moved out of the share screener, because a cash flow valuation doesn't fit a company whose assets are other shares.

LICs are judged on the share price against net tangible assets (NTA), fee and performance fee, dividends and total return. Unlike an ETF, an LIC can't create or cancel shares to keep its price near its NTA, so it can trade at a lasting discount or premium.
Most Australian LICs pay fully franked dividends; the yields shown are cash only, before franking.

entries.title: Net tangible assets (NTA)
entries.definition: What an LIC's investments are worth per share, less its liabilities, as the company reports it each month. Pre-tax NTA is before tax on gains not yet realised.
entries.hover: The value per share of what the LIC holds, net of liabilities, before tax on unrealised gains, at the NTA date in the ASX report (usually the end of the month before).

entries.title: Premium/discount to NTA
entries.definition: How far an LIC's share price sits above (premium) or below (discount) its net tangible assets per share. A discount means buying its investments for less than they're worth.
entries.hover: Latest share price against the last reported NTA. A discount buys the LIC's investments for less than their value; it can persist or widen, so check why. The ASX report's own figure is at its NTA date.

entries.title: Performance fee
entries.definition: A fee some LIC managers charge on top of the management fee when returns beat a benchmark. Yes or No, from the ASX report.

entries.title: Market cap
entries.definition: Market capitalisation: shares on issue times the share price, from the ASX report. For an LIC it differs from the value of its investments by the premium or discount to NTA.

entries.title: LIC screener
entries.definition: Every LIC and LIT Sift follows, with its premium or discount to NTA, fee, performance fee, market cap, returns and yield, kept apart from shares and ETFs.
body: Sorted by premium or discount to NTA, deepest discount first; click any heading to sort by it, and a row to open the LIC.
Filter by category (the ASX's grouping, such as Equity - Australia or Fixed Income - Australian Dollar), by watchlist, or to the LICs you hold. LIT marks a listed investment trust.
There are no suggested actions or scores for LICs: those come from estimated value. The discount to NTA is the value measure instead.

entries.title: An LIC's page
entries.definition: Everything about one LIC: share price, premium or discount to NTA, fee, yield, performance against its category and an LIC you choose, growth of $10,000, NTA history, dividends and company facts.
body: The premium or discount tile compares the latest share price with the last NTA in the ASX report; the company facts also give the ASX's figure at the NTA date.
Premium/discount to NTA over time builds as each month's report is loaded.
Performance, growth of $10,000 and dividends work as on an ETF's page; the reference starts as the largest other LIC in the same category.

entries.title: Real estate investment trust (REIT)
entries.definition: A listed trust that owns income-producing property.

entries.title: Country
entries.definition: Country of domicile from Yahoo Finance; outside Australia means no franking credits.
entries.hover: Country of domicile from Yahoo Finance. Companies outside Australia are treated as paying no franking credits.

entries.title: Reporting currency
entries.definition: The currency a company publishes its financial statements in, which can differ from the currency its shares trade in on the ASX.
entries.hover: The currency the company publishes its financial statements in. Statements in another currency (US dollars for most large miners, New Zealand dollars for NZ listings) are converted into the share price's currency at the exchange rate on each report's balance date, so earnings, book value, cash flow and every ratio built on them compare like with like. Dividends are already in the share price's currency and are not converted.

entries.title: Yes (Y)
entries.definition: The company passes the test.

entries.title: No (N)
entries.definition: The company fails the test.

entries.title: Model and rules (admin)
entries.definition: Every setting behind Sift's results, the formula each feeds, and a lab for trying other values.
body: Open it from your avatar menu (top right), under Model and rules. Settings and formulas lists every adjustable setting with its live value, allowed range, formula and where it's used, grouped as valuation models, the four value tests, markers and actions, and the score wheel.

What-if scenarios lets you change any of them and see what would happen on today's data. Nothing live changes: the nightly job, the screener, your actions and the track record keep using the live settings.
Every company page has Show workings: each step behind its figures, with its own numbers.

entries.title: Scenario (what-if)
entries.definition: A named set of changed settings, run against today's data to see what would change, without changing anything live.
body: Leave a setting blank to keep its live value. Run shows: how many companies get each action, live against the scenario; which move between actions; the spread of margins of safety; every company whose action or valuation status changes; and what happens to your holdings and watchlists.
The margin-of-safety trend (momentum) stays at its live value in a scenario, because it compares with the live figure stored 30 days ago. Holdings and watchlists are today's.
A scenario uses today's data only; it can't say how the settings would have done in the past.

entries.title: Show workings
entries.definition: On every company page: each step behind its estimated value, ratios, tests, markers and action, with its own numbers.
body: The valuation steps show the base averaged over the years used, each year's projected cash flow and present value, the terminal value, cash and debt, shares on issue, the estimated value and the margin of safety.
Choose a saved scenario at the top to see the same company under other settings.

entries.title: Sensitivity grid
entries.definition: A company's estimated value and margin of safety across a range of discount rates and growth rates.
body: Rows are growth rates around the model's own, columns are discount rates from 7% to 11%. The outlined cell is the setting in use. Wide swings across the grid mean the estimate leans heavily on its assumptions, so treat its margin of safety with care.

entries.title: Growth rate (valuation)
entries.definition: How fast a valuation model assumes cash flow (DCF) or dividends (DDM) grow each year for the first five years, before the terminal value takes over.
body: Live: 8% a year for free cash flow and 5% a year for dividends, set in Model and rules. A higher rate raises the estimated value; Show workings and the sensitivity grid show by how much for each company.

entries.title: Analyst ratings
entries.definition: How many broker analysts rate a share strong buy, buy, hold, sell or strong sell, month by month, as collected by Yahoo Finance.
body: The consensus is Yahoo's average of the ratings on a scale of 1 (strong buy) to 5 (strong sell). Sift shows the latest four months so you can see whether opinion is moving.
Analyst ratings are shown for context only. They play no part in Sift's estimated value, scores, tests or suggested actions, which stay Sift's own analysis.
Coverage of ASX companies is patchy: smaller companies often have no analysts, and the counts can lag local broker changes. Refreshed weekly.

entries.title: Analyst price targets
entries.definition: The share price analysts expect in about 12 months: the lowest, average, median and highest of their targets, as collected by Yahoo Finance.
body: The bar spans the lowest to highest target, with today's price, the average target and Sift's estimated value marked on it. A wide bar means analysts disagree.
A price target is a 12-month price forecast, not an estimate of intrinsic value, so it can differ a lot from Sift's estimated value. Shown for context only and refreshed weekly.

entries.title: Major holders
entries.hover: Who owns the company, from Yahoo Finance: the share held by insiders (directors and executives) and by institutions, and the largest fund and institutional holders.
entries.definition: Who owns the company, as collected by Yahoo Finance: the share held by insiders and by institutions, and the ten largest mutual fund and institutional holders.
body: Insiders are directors, executives and large related holders. Institutions (% of float) counts only the shares that trade freely, so it can be higher than the plain institutions figure.

The holder lists come mainly from overseas fund filings, so global funds (such as Vanguard's international funds) appear while Australian super funds are often missing. Treat them as a partial view, not a share register.
Value now is each holding at today's share price. Change is how much the holder added or sold since their previous report. Refreshed weekly.

entries.title: Coattail investing
entries.definition: Coattail investing simply means letting the "smart money" do the heavy lifting, then copying their moves.
body: The term comes from the everyday phrase "riding on someone's coattails": tagging along right behind a successful person so you can benefit from their effort and momentum.

In plain English: instead of spending hours researching financial reports yourself, you watch what famous investors or large hedge funds (such as Warren Buffett or Ray Dalio) buy and sell, and then make the same trades in your own account. You're effectively using their multi-million-dollar research teams and expertise to guide your own choices.

In Sift: the Coattail page focuses on the ASX. It shows the fund managers holding the screener's companies, such as Vanguard and BlackRock, with what each holds and what it bought or sold. ASX director trades (Appendix 3Y notices) and substantial holder notices (stakes of 5% or more) are coming next. Famous US investors' portfolios, from their quarterly 13F filings, are noted for later.

Keep in mind: holdings are reported after the event, often weeks or months later; you see what they bought but not why, or when they'll sell; and their time frame and position size may differ from yours. Their moves are a lead for your own research, alongside Sift's valuation, not a replacement for it.

entries.title: Who's investing
entries.definition: The fund managers holding the screener's companies, each with the companies it holds and what it bought or sold since its previous report.
entries.hover: Shares bought (+) or sold (-) since this holder's previous report. New means a new, or nearly new, holding. Hover the figure for the percentage change.
body: Source: the top 10 fund and top 10 institutional holders Yahoo Finance lists for each screener company, refreshed weekly (a seventh of the companies each night). So a manager appears for a company only when it's in that company's top 10, and only screener companies are covered: Vanguard and BlackRock hold far more than the cards show. The lists come mostly from overseas funds' own filings, so Australian super funds are often missing, and each holding is as at its report date. The page says how many screener companies have holder lists so far.

Holders are grouped by the manager behind them: Vanguard's index funds and Vanguard Group Inc are one Vanguard card; iShares funds are BlackRock; DFA funds are Dimensional. Each card shows the value of its listed holdings in screener companies at today's prices, the average score wheel of the companies it holds, a few of them, and how many it's adding to and cutting. Sort the cards by companies held, adding, cutting or value held, and search or filter them like the other lists: by holder, companies held, adding, cutting, value held, or the companies it holds (Holds). Click a card for every company it holds.

On a holder's page each company appears once, through the manager's largest listed holding in it (an institution's figure usually includes its own funds, so they aren't added up). Value now is those shares at today's price.
Change is the number of shares bought or sold since that holder's previous report, worked out from its holding and Yahoo's percentage change.

Where the funds are going counts, for each company, how many managers added and how many cut. Most added to has more adding than cutting, Most cut the reverse. Click a number to see the managers behind it, with the shares each bought or sold; click it again to close. Recommendation is Sift's own suggested action for the company: where the managers and Sift agree, the case is stronger; where they disagree, it's worth a closer look.

Index funds and ETFs buy and sell to match their index, not because of a view on the company. They're shown by default, since managers such as Vanguard and BlackRock hold mostly through them; tick Hide index funds to leave them out. Sift spots them by name (index, ETF, iShares, SPDR, MSCI and similar), so a few may slip through. Use Reported to keep to recent filings. A holder's page says how many companies the filters hide, with a Show all button.

Value held is not funds under management: it counts only the holdings Yahoo lists in screener companies. A manager's total funds under management (Vanguard's runs to trillions of dollars) isn't in Sift's data.

entries.title: Filtering a table
entries.definition: Every list in Sift (the share, ETF and LIC screeners, each watchlist, each portfolio's holdings, and Coattail's holder cards) can be searched and filtered by any column.
body: Search: the box above the table finds rows whose text in any column contains what you type, such as BHP, Materials or 60%.

Right-click any cell (press and hold on a phone) for Show matching (only rows with that value), Filter out (hide them), and for numbers Greater than or Less than that value. A blank cell offers rows with or without a value.

Filter (the pink button) opens the condition builder: pick a column, a condition (equals, contains, greater than, between, is empty and so on) and a value. Numbers can be typed as 20, 20%, $1.2B or 300k; separate several values with commas, such as BHP, RIO. Add conditions with AND or OR; they apply top to bottom, so A AND B OR C means (A AND B) OR C. A condition still being typed is shown dashed and not applied yet.
Each active filter shows as a chip under the controls: click it to remove it, or Clear all. The table's quick filters (action, sector, category, watchlist, Held only) still work alongside.
Each table keeps its own filters while you move around Sift; they clear when the page reloads. Opening a screener from a dashboard link starts it without them.

entries.title: Searching Sift
entries.definition: The search box in the menu bar finds anything in Sift: shares, ETFs, LICs, fund managers, your watchlists and portfolios, help articles, pages and settings.
body: Everything or this page: the pink ▾ beside the magnifying glass chooses. The dashboard and the results page search everything; every other page searches itself by default. Admins have a third choice, Developer knowledge base, which searches only the developer articles; they're never mixed into Everything.

This page: on a list (the screener, ETFs, LICs, Coattail, a watchlist or portfolio) the words go into that list's search box; on Help, into the help search; on any other page they're highlighted where they appear, and Enter again moves to the next. If they're not on the page, Sift shows results from everywhere instead.

Everything: an exact ASX code opens that company or fund straight away; anything else opens the results page. Each word can be the start of a word (wes finds Wesfarmers) and plurals match (dividends finds dividend). Small typos are forgiven when the exact words find little (vangaurd finds Vanguard).

Results: the best 100, exact codes and titles first, with the matched words highlighted. Tick boxes down the left narrow them by type, sector or category, recommendation, Mine (held, on a watchlist, your lists) and knowledge article topic, each with a count; ticking one box never hides the others in its group. On a phone, Filters opens the tick boxes.

Kept up to date: the index is rebuilt after each nightly run, your own watchlists, portfolios and scenarios the moment you save them, and help and pages each time Sift starts. Rebuild it now from Admin, Search, or in PowerShell with .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m src.search.reindex.

Getting better with use: each search is noted, with which result you opened. Results opened and given a pink thumbs up rise for the same words next time; a thumbs down makes one sink. Click a thumb again to take your vote back.

Synonyms: Admin, Search lets you say that terms mean the same, such as cba = commonwealth bank, so searching one finds the others. Search insights there lists the top searches, searches that found nothing (usually fixed with a synonym) and results marked not what was wanted.

Meaning-based (AI) search is built in but switched off: once on, Sift also finds things by meaning, not just words, using a small model that runs inside Sift so nothing leaves your PC. Admin, Search says how to switch it on.

entries.title: Your profile and preferences
entries.definition: The round avatar at the top right opens your Profile, Preferences and Keyboard shortcuts. Preferences are saved to your account, so they follow you to any browser.
body: Profile: your display name (how Sift greets you and how admins see you) and email. The email changes with sign-in, coming in a later release.
Display: compact spacing fits more on the screen; wrapping shows long names in full; help tips are the small "i" beside terms.
Theme: light, dark, or system (follows your device).

Accessibility: reduce motion turns animations off; patterns as well as colours dash the lines and hatch the bars in charts so they can be told apart without colour; data tables opens the table under every chart; show all buttons shows the buttons that otherwise appear on hover; keyboard shortcuts can be turned off.
User experience: the page Sift opens on, what the search box searches until you change it with the pink ▾, and how many rows long tables show before "Show more".

Keyboard shortcuts: "/" to search, "?" for the list, and "g" then a letter to go somewhere: d Dashboard, s Screener, e ETFs, l LICs, w Watchlists, p Portfolios, t Track record, c Coattail, h Help, f Preferences.
Reset all to defaults (top of Preferences) puts every preference back.

entries.title: Users and impersonation (admins)
entries.definition: Admins manage accounts in Admin, Users, and can impersonate a member: see and use Sift exactly as that person does, to help them or check what they see.
body: Accounts: each person has their own portfolios, watchlists, scenarios, layout and preferences. Market data, valuations and help are shared.
Add an account with an email, display name and role. Members use Sift; admins also manage its settings and accounts. Until sign-in arrives, a new account can be used only through Impersonate.
Make admin, Make member, Disable and Enable change an account. Nobody can remove their own admin role or disable themselves, and Sift always keeps at least one active admin.

Impersonate (from the avatar menu or a row in Users): everything you see and change is as that person. A banner shows on every page with End impersonation. The admin console is closed meanwhile, as it is for them. Admins can't be impersonated, nor can disabled accounts.
Safeguards: a session ends by itself after 8 hours, and ends if the person is disabled or made an admin. Every session is kept in the impersonation log: who, as whom, when, and how it ended.

entries.title: Developer knowledge base (admins)
entries.definition: Admins have a developer knowledge base under Admin, Developer: how Sift is designed and how it works, for diagnosing problems, planning improvements and handing work to a helper.
body: Articles: start here (overview, architecture, setup, testing, how changes are made), one article per feature, data, operations runbooks for common problems, and decision records explaining why Sift is built the way it is.
Generated reference pages are built from Sift itself each time they're opened, so they're always current: the data dictionary, every API route, every setting, dependencies and the test catalogue.
The improvement register lists known issues, technical debt, ideas and risks, with priority and status. Release notes record each version of Sift.
Each article shows its version, owner, published and last reviewed dates and when it's next due for review; overdue reviews show on the home page.

Articles are kept with the code in git (docs/kb), so they change with it. Only admins can open them. To search them, choose Developer knowledge base in the search box's pink menu (the default on these pages); they're never mixed into Everything.
